Cobalt-Catalyzed C8-Dienylation of Quinoline-N-Oxides
Rahul K. Shukla, AkshayM .N air,S alman Khan, and Chandra M. R. Volla*
Abstract: An efficient Cp*CoIII-catalyzed C8-dienylation of
quinoline-N-oxides was achieved by employing allenes bearing
leaving groups at the a-position as the dienylating agents.T he
reaction proceeds by CoIII-catalyzed C@Ha ctivation of
quinoline-N-oxides and regioselective migratory insertion of
the allene followed by a b-oxy elimination, leading to overall
dienylation. Site-selective C@Ha ctivation was achieved with
excellent selectivity under mild reaction conditions,a nd
30 mol %o faN aF additive was found to be crucial for the
efficient dienylation. The methodology features high stereose-
lectivity,m ild reaction conditions,a nd good functional-group
tolerance.C 8-alkenylation of quinoline-N-oxides was achieved
in the case of allenes devoid of leaving groups as coupling
partners.F urthermore,g ram-scale preparation and prelimi-
nary mechanistic experiments were carried out to gain insights
into the reaction mechanism.
Introduction
Allenes have emerged as valuable scaffolds in synthetic
organic chemistry and have been widely studied in av ariety of
carbocyclization and cross-coupling reactions.[1] Ther ecent
years have witnessed ar emarkable surge in the study of
allenes as coupling partners in transition metal catalyzed C@H
activation reactions.[2] Thep resence of two orthogonal double
bonds in an allene moiety gives rise to av ariety of
regioselective and chemoselective disparities,w hich impart
significant challenges for engaging allenes in transition metal
mediated reactions,a nd at the same time provide ample
opportunities to generate rapid molecular complexity by
exploiting their unique reactivity patterns.[3] Fore xample,
depending on the stereoelectronic nature of the allene and the
choice of the metal catalyst M,t he organometallic intermedi-
ate R-M generated after C@Ha ctivation, could follow two
distinct migratory insertion pathways (Scheme 1a ). The1 ,2-
insertion of R-M on the allene would lead to the metal alkenyl
intermediate Int-I,w hile the carbometallation with the C2=
C3 double bond of allenes leads to the p-allyl intermediate
Int-II.[4] Both these intermediates are highly reactive and
undergo av ariety of termination steps such as protonation, b-
hydride elimination, reductive elimination, or Tsuji—Trost-
type nucleophilic addition resulting in an assortment of
products.C apitalizing on these complementary reactivities,
av ariety of C@Hf unctionalization reactions like alkenylation,
allenylation, and other reactions have been reported, employ-
ing precious second- and third-row transition-metal catalysts
like IrIII,R hIII,R uII,a nd PdII.[5–8]
Theq uest for efficient and sustainable catalysis,h as led to
the emergence of low-cost and environmentally benign first-
row transition metals as worthy catalysts in C@Hf unctional-
izations.[9,1 0] Amidst the renaissance in earth-abundant metal
catalysis,c obalt has emerged as an evident choice for the
development of C@Hf unctionalization protocols because of
its higher Lewis acidity and good selectivity.[11] Av ariety of
C@Hf unctionalization reactions using both low-valent and
high-valent cobalt catalysts have been reported in the recent
years.H owever,t he relevance of ac obalt catalysis for C@H
functionalization with allenes has been infrequently reported
and the reactivity is so far limited to alkenylation and
annulation reactions (Scheme 1b ).[12] Ackermann and co-
workers illustrated an elegant C@Ha lkenylation with allenes
originating from cobalt alkenyl pathway (Int-I).[13] Later, the
complementary cobalt-allyl intermediate generated from
allenes was explored by Cheng and co-workers to describe

[3++3] and [5++1] annulation reactions.[14] In this regard, we
recently reported ac obalt catalyzed [4++2] annulation reac-
tion of allenes and benzamides for the regioselective synthesis
of dihydroiso quinolinones.[15] We observed that the reaction
proceeds via aC o-s-allyl complex formed by the regioselec-
tive migratory insertion of the arylcobalt(III)-intermediate
with the C2=C3 double bond of allenes.T og ain more
understanding on this mechanistic rationale and to expand
the chemical space,w ee nvisioned installing al eaving group at
the allylic position of the allene for allowing af acile b-oxy
elimination to realize ac atalytic dienylation under oxidant-
free conditions.W hile the transition metal catalyzed C@H
allylation reactions have been extensively studied, the
corresponding C@Hd ienylation reactions to access function-
alized 1,3-dienes were largely ignored, despite their high
relevance in organic synthesis and materials science.[16] The
traditional methods for accessing dienes involve Wittig/HWE
reactions or transition metal mediated cross-coupling reac-
tions.[17] However these reactions often require prefunction-
alized substrates and suffer from poor stereo- and regiose-
lectivity.C onsequently,t he development of suitable dienylat-
ing agents for regioselective introduction of diene fragment
into organic molecules is of utmost importance.[18]
At the same time,f unctionalization of quinoline at various
positions is of prime interest to both medicinal and synthetic
chemists alike.[19] Thes ite-selective transformations of quin-
oline at the C2(H) position is well explored because of its
acidic nature.[20] However,o nly ah andful of reports exist
documenting C8(H) functionalization of quinolines.[21] Selec-
tive C8 functionalization of quinoline-N-oxides using tran-
sition-metal catalysts has gained significant attention in the
recent years.O wing to the importance of both functionalized
1,3-dienes and quinolines in medicinal chemistry,w ee nvi-
sioned developing as ite-selective catalytic dienylation of
quinoline-N-oxides using allenylcarbinol carbonates as the
dienylating agents.B ased on our previous work, we antici-
pated that the Co-s-allyl complex formed after regioselective
2,3-migratory insertion will undergo facile b-oxy elimination,
leading to C2-functionalized dienes (Scheme 1c ).
Results and Discussion
Identification of the Leaving Group
To facilitate af acile b-oxy elimination from aC oIII-s-allyl-
intermediate,t he allenyl alcohol 2 was chosen as the
dienlylating agent (Scheme 2). To our delight, the C8-
dienylated quinoline-N-oxide 7a was afforded in 20 %w hen
1a was reacted with 2 using 10 mol %o fC p*Co(CO)I2 and
30 mol %o fN aOPiv in TFE at 90 88Cf or 12 hours.D elighted
with this,w ee mployed the allenyl acetate 3 instead of 2 in
reaction with 1a and 7a was obtained in an improved yield of
41 %. This motivated us to further screen various leaving
groups on the allene (Scheme 2) and among these leaving
groups,a se xpected, carbonate was found to be most
favorable for the present transformation as allenyl carbinol
carbonate 5 delivered 7a in 54 %a nd the tert-butyl carbonate
(Boc) 6 led to the product in 55 %.
Optimization of the Reaction Conditions
To achieve further amplification in yield, as olvent screen-
ing was carried out and we observed that the reaction
proceeds more proficiently in TFE compared to other
solvents like MeOH, DCE, HFIP (Table 1, entries 1–6).
Inquisitively,w hen the effect of various bases was studied,
we found that NaOPiv was optimal for the dienylation
(entries 7a nd 8). Further,w ei nvestigated the consequence of
ionization by the addition of silver salts.A ddition of 30 mol %
of AgOTf furnished the dienylation product 7a in 60 %
(entry 10) and 30 mol %o fA gSbF6 led to the product in 55 %
(entry 11). Interestingly,a substantial amplification in yield
was observed when KF (78 %) was used as an additive
(entry 12) and captivatingly,t he yield increased to 88 %( 82 %
upon isolation) when NaF was employed (entry 13). With

found the optimized reaction conditions to be the following:
1e quivalent of 1a and 1.2 equivalents of 5a in the presence of

30 mol %o fN aF in TFE at 90 88Ca ffords 7a in 82 %.
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we
investigated the scope of various diversely substituted quin-
oline-N-oxides (Table 2), which could participate in the
dienylation reaction. Alkyl groups on various positions of
the N-oxide were well tolerated, giving excellent yields of the
corresponding products (7b —e,8 2–89 %). While electron-
rich quinoline-N-oxides having alkyl and methoxy groups
provided the corresponding products in good yields,m oderate
yields were observed for the electron-deficient counterparts
(7g –j in 45–60 %). To our delight, quinoline-N-oxides bearing
precarious functional groups such as nitro (1i), ester (1j ), and
alkyne (1k )f urnished the respective products 7i –k,a lbeit in
slightly diminished yields.M oreover,t he disubstituted quin-
oline N-oxide 1l was also found to be an amenable substrate
providing 7l in 88 %. Quinoline-N-oxides bearing an array of
electronically diverse 3-aryl substituents furnished the corre-
sponding products 7m –q in good yields (67–91 %). Remark-
ably,t he reaction can be extended for C5- and C8-dienyla-
tions of the benzo[f]quinoline-N-oxide 1q and quinoxaline N-
oxide 1r ,r espectively,a ffording the corresponding products
7q (75 %) and 7r (65 %). However,t etrahydroquinoline-N-
oxide (7s )a nd 2-vinyl-pyridine-N-oxide (7t )w ere found to be
ineffective indicating that the dienylation is selective for
quinoline-N-oxides.
Next the scope of the developed protocol was studied
against an array of allenyl carbinol carbonates (Table 3).
Allenes bearing alkyl chains of increasing chain length (R =
methyl, n-propyl, n-butyl, n-pentyl and n-hexyl) fared well for
the reaction furnishing the corresponding dienes 7u –y in 73–
81 %. While the branched allene furnished the product 7z in

70 %y ield, 7a a was obtained in 75 %w hen benzyl-substituted
allene was employed. Allenes bearing electronically diverse
phenyl rings were also found to be amenable furnishing the
corresponding 1,3-diarylated 1,3-dienes 7a b–al in 53–74 %
yields.T he reaction was also extended to internal allenes to
isolate the corresponding diene 7a m in 69 %. Further,w e
found the protocol was amenable for late-stage modifications
of complex natural products.A llenes tethered to menthol and
cholesterol furnished the corresponding dienes 7a n (65 %)
and 7a o (60 %) in good yields.
To epitomize the utility of the protocol, we envisioned
as equential hetero-bisfunctionalization of quinoline-N-oxide
by carrying out aP dII-catalyzed C2-alkylation followed by
CoIII-catalyzed C8-dienylation. Pd-catalyzed C2-alkylation of
6-methoxy quinoline-N-oxide (1f )w as considered based on
the work of Wu and co-workers[22] with 1,4-dioxane and
tetrahydrofuran to access the corresponding C2-functional-
ized quinoline-N-oxides 8a and 8b,r espectively.C oIII-cata-
lyzed dienylation of 8 with 5a led to the smooth formation of
C2- and C8-functionalized 6-methoxyquinoline N-oxides 9a
and 9b,r espectively,i ng ood yields (Scheme 3a ). Ag ram-
scale reaction was performed to probe the synthetic utility of
the developed reaction. When 1.0 gram of 1a was reacted
with 1.06 grams of 5a under the standard reaction conditions,
1.11 grams of 7a were obtained in 82 %y ield, showing the
practicality of the dienylation (Scheme 3b ). Quinoline N-
oxide acts as at raceless directing group that allows further
diversification at late stages by keeping the butadiene frag-
ment intact as depicted in Scheme 3c .R eduction of the
quinoline N-oxides to synthetically more relevant quinolines
was achieved on treatment with PCl3 to isolate 10 a and 10 b in
62 %a nd 69 %, respectively.I na ddition, reaction of 7b with
acetic anhydride led to the clean transposition of the oxy
functionality to the a-carbon atom, affording the a-acetoxy-
substituted quinaldine 11 in 96 %y ield. Given the importance
of both quinolines and triazoles in medicinal chemistry,i t
could be expected that their conjugates could exhibit
significant pharmacological activities.W ith this in mind, we
explored the reactivity of C8-dienylated quinoline N-oxides
with N-sulfonylated 1,2,3-triazoles and we were delighted to
observe the formation of the 2-triazolyl quinolines 13 a (95 %)
and 13 b (86 %) in excellent yields by treating 7 with triazole
12.[23] Thes tructure and regioselectivity were unambiguously
confirmed by the single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis of
13 b.F urther, an intermolecular Diels–Alder reaction of 1,3-
diene 10 a with diethyl acetylene dicarboxylate proceeded
efficiently in toluene at 80 88Ct oa fford cyclic 1,4-diene 14 a in
90 %y ield. Additionally,c atalytic hydrogenation of 13 a using
20 mol %o fP d/C provided the formal alkylation product 15
in 95 %y ield.
Subsequently,t og ain insights on the reaction mechanism
and to expand the synthetic applicability,w et ested the
reactivity of allenes,d evoid of al eaving group at the b-
position, for the CoIII-catalyzed C@Ha ctivation of quinoline
N-oxides (1). We were pleased to observe that treating 1 with
the cyclohexyl allene 16 using 10 mol %[ Cp*Co(CO)I2]i n
TFE led to the formation of the C8-alkenylated quinoline N-
oxides 17 a,b in moderate yields (50–55 %; Scheme 4). This
result could be attributed to the protonation of the cobalt-s-
allyl intermediate originating from the 2,3-insertion on to the
allene.T he formation of both 7 and 17 suggests the tendency
of arylcobalt(III)-intermediate to undergo regioselective 2,3-
migratory insertion with allenes.
To shed light on to the reaction mechanism, as eries of
preliminary mechanistic studies were performed. TheC 8-
deuterated quinoline N-oxide [D]-1a (91 %D )w as synthe-
sized in 98 %b yR hIII-catalyzed C@Ha ctivation of 1a in the
presence of 1:1m ixture of DCE and CH3COOD (Sche-
me 5a ). Deuterium-exchange studies were carried out under
the standard reaction conditions with 1a and [D]-1a and no
deuterium incorporation was detected at the C8-position,
with or without 5a ,s uggesting that the C@Hb ond cleavage
(C@Ha ctivation) is irreversible (Scheme 5b –d). Further,
competitive experiments with 6-Me- and 6-NO2-substituted
quinoline-N-oxides with 5a indicated ap reference for the
electron-rich 6-Me derivative,p robably because of its better
coordinating ability compared to 6-NO2 derivative (Sche-
me 5e ). Ac ompetitive isotopic value (kH/kD)o f1 .34 was

Finally,p arallel reactions of 1a or C8-[D]-1a with 5a showed

Based on our mechanistic studies,t he plausible mecha-
nism for the CoIII-catalyzed dienylation is proposed as shown
in Scheme 6. Ionization of Cp*Co(CO)I2 in the presence of
sodium carboxylate and sodium fluoride forms the catalyti-
cally active CoIII-complex A.C oordination of 1 with A
proceeds through electron-rich oxygen, followed by site-
selective C@Ha ctivation at the C8-position, leading to the
cyclometalated complex C.C oordination of C with allenyl
carbinol carbonate 5 followed by regioselective migratory
insertion with C2=C3 double bond leads to the intermediate
E.F inally,f acile b-oxy elimination from E furnishes the
dienylated product 7,l eading to overall dienylation.
Conclusion
In conclusion, we have developed the first cobalt-cata-
lyzed regioselective C8 dienylation of quinoline N-oxides,
employing allenylcarbinol carbonates as the dienylating
agents.T he reaction displays broad substrate scope with good
to excellent yields against av ariety of diversely substituted
quinoline N-oxides and allenes under relatively mild reaction
conditions.T he utility of the protocol was justified by the
facile scalability and further synthetic transformation of the
products.F urthermore,t oe xpand the generality of the
protocol, 1,2,3-triazole conjugates of the dienylated quino-
lines were synthesized in excellent yields.C ompetitive experi-
ments and deuterium-labeling studies were carried out shed
light on the reaction mechanism.
